claims.claim_text: Wallach calls red meat an unequaled source of animal protein and essential lipids; the only trick is to cook it no more than medium, since well-done or burnt fat forms heterocyclic amines. He even recommends raw steak tartare. In his words: "Red meat is an unequaled source of animal protein and essential lipids"
claims.verbatim:
Red meat is an unequaled source of animal protein and essential 
lipids - the secret is to not eat meat cooked well done or eat the fat 
burnt as they become heterocyclic amines. Medium rare and me- 
dium are the safe way to eat beef. Steak Tartar is a half pound of raw, 
freshly ground sirloin, served with chopped onions, pepper corns 
and topped with a raw egg - it doesn’t get any better than this!

claims.claim_text: Wallach cites a 930-woman study where eating beef and pork very well done raised breast-cancer risk 462% versus medium-rare; his point is that it is not the fat but the cooking that harms you, because burnt animal fat becomes heterocyclic amines, powerful carcinogens. In his words: "Burnt animal fat is converted to heterocyclic amines which are extremely powerful carcinogens"
claims.verbatim:
On November 18, 1998, Dr. Wei Zheng of the University of South 
Carolina reported that in a study of 930 women, those who ate their 
beef and pork cooked very well done increased their risk of breast 
cancer by 462 percent over those women who ate their meat cooked 
medium rare - it is not the amount of fat in the diet that counts, but 
rather, how you cook the fat that counts. Burnt animal fat is con- 
verted to heterocyclic amines which are extremely powerful carcino- 
gens.

claims.claim_text: Wallach's 'Feedlot Syndrome' analogy: ranchers fatten beef cattle on a steady stream of carbohydrate feed paired with optimal nutrients that drive the animal to eat with endless, fervent hunger, growing a 40-lb calf to 900-1,100 lb in a year. He argues humans are fattened by the same carb-heavy diet — but, unlike the optimally-supplemented cattle, humans eat it while mineral-deficient, which is what leaves them with a ravenous appetite. In his words: "Beef cattle will grow from a forty pound calf to 900 - 1,100 pounds in about a year under optimal feedlot conditions"
claims.verbatim:
Raising prime beef successfully, requires a steady stream of car- 
bohydrate, protein and fat calories in the proper ratios specifically 
designed for fattening. 
The intense weight gain, high carbohydrate diet must be accom- 
panied by optimal mixes of nutrients designed to encourage weight 
gain and drive the animal to eat with an endless and fervent hunger. 
Feed, based on corn or other carbohydrates, is made available in 
a steady stream. Beef cattle will grow from a forty pound calf to 900 
- 1,100 pounds in about a year under optimal feedlot conditions.

claims.claim_text: Not on its own, in Wallach's view. He points to the Old Order Amish, who eat pork, beef, goat and mutton 3 times a day plus heavy whole milk, butter and cheese — by his account consuming more sugar, fat, red meat and dairy than anyone in North America — and yet post an obesity rate of just 4% and a type-II diabetes rate of just 6%, only about a tenth and a half, respectively, of their 'modern' neighbors in the very same county. He credits that gap not to their meat-heavy diet, and not even to their hard farm labor (the horses do most of the work), but to the essential minerals in the wood ashes they spread on their garden soil every single morning. In his words: "they eat pork, beef, goat and mutton three times each day"

Wallach cites a Scientific American longevity summary: the patients who followed doctors' advice to the letter didn't reach 100, while the 'rebellious' ones who ate salt, eggs, red meat, butter and chicken skin did. In his words: "people who ate salt, eggs, red meat, butter and chicken skin did."

claims.claim_text: Pellagra turned out to be a dietary deficiency disease — a lack of vitamin B3 (niacin) — and eggs were part of the fix. Wallach recounts how a U.S. Public Health Service researcher noticed that in orphanages and mental asylums the residents came down with pellagra while the staff, who ate a wider variety of food, stayed well. When eggs and milk were simply added to the sufferers' diets, the pellagra disappeared. That result pointed to a missing dietary factor rather than the infection that most people of the era assumed, and it is Wallach's illustration that nutrient-dense foods like eggs can reverse a 'disease' that was really malnutrition. In his words: "When eggs and milk were added to the diet of the affected individuals, pellagra disappeared."

claims.claim_text: Yes — and it was more than a footnote. Wallach was a co-petitioner on the FDA petition (Docket No. 03Q-0401, filed 6/23/2003) that won the qualified health claim linking omega-3 fatty acids to reduced coronary heart disease risk, which the FDA allowed on 9/8/2004. It matters because it was one front in Wallach's larger legal war against the FDA — waged with First Amendment attorney Jonathan Emord — to force the agency to let supplement makers state health benefits that were actually proven. The same campaign carried his solo selenium-and-cancer claim (approved 4/28/2003); as he tells it, after losing every battle before the 1994 DSHEA Act, his side won every one that followed. So the official omega-3 heart-health language products can now use is partly his doing. In his words: "qualified claim allowed by FDA on 9/8/2004"
